presentingComplaint: Right-sided facial pain and pressure with purulent nasal discharge for 12 days, worsening again after an initial partial improvement, despite a completed course of amoxicillin.
history: A 46-year-old woman presents with a 12-day history of nasal congestion, thick yellow-green nasal discharge and right maxillary/periorbital facial pain and pressure that worsens on bending forward. The illness began like a coryzal URTI; she improved briefly around day 6 but then deteriorated ("double sickening") with recrudescent high fever, escalating unilateral facial pain and postnasal purulence. Her GP started oral amoxicillin 500 mg TDS on day 7 for presumed acute bacterial rhinosinusitis; she completed 5 days with no meaningful improvement and symptoms have progressed. She has type 2 diabetes (last HbA1c 8.4%) and had a course of co-amoxiclav for a dental infection three months ago. No visual change, no diplopia, no periorbital swelling, no neck stiffness, no altered behaviour. Non-smoker; lives in Pune, no recent travel. NKDA.
examination: Alert, mildly unwell but not toxic. Tenderness over the right maxillary and frontal sinuses with reproduction of pain on percussion. Anterior rhinoscopy shows congested, oedematous right middle meatus with mucopurulent discharge tracking from the osteomeatal complex. No periorbital erythema, no proptosis, extraocular movements full and painless, pupils equal and reactive. Oropharynx shows posterior purulent drainage. Neck supple; no focal neurological deficit. Chest clear.
imaging: CT paranasal sinuses (non-contrast): near-complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus with an air-fluid level, mucosal thickening of the right ethmoid air cells and obstruction of the right osteomeatal complex. No bony erosion, no orbital or intracranial extension.
microbiology: Endoscopically guided middle-meatal aspirate obtained by ENT: Gram stain shows Gram-negative coccobacilli and Gram-positive diplococci. Culture grows beta-lactamase-producing Haemophilus influenzae (ampicillin-resistant, amoxicillin-clavulanate susceptible) plus penicillin-non-susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin MIC 4 mg/L, ceftriaxone susceptible, levofloxacin susceptible). Blood cultures negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis with a resistant organism after amoxicillin failure (leading diagnosis)
Prolonged viral upper respiratory tract infection
finalDiagnosis: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (right maxillary/ethmoid) failing first-line amoxicillin, culture-confirmed beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae and penicillin-non-susceptible S. pneumoniae, managed with antibiotic escalation and ENT sinus drainage (source control).
citations: IDSA Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis Clinical Practice Guideline 2012
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Pharyngitis, Sinusitis, Otitis, and Other Upper Respiratory Tract Infections
AAO-HNS Adult Sinusitis Clinical Practice Guideline (Update) 2015
stewardship: Diagnosis rests on bacterial ABRS criteria: symptoms >10 days without improvement plus the 'double sickening' pattern with purulent discharge, unilateral facial pain and fever — not a simple viral URTI. First-line high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate is preferred over amoxicillin alone precisely because of beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae and penicillin-non-susceptible pneumococcus, both present here; plain amoxicillin failure was predictable given the amoxicillin monotherapy and recent antibiotic exposure. Escalation: switch to high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate 2 g/125 mg BD (extended-release) for 7-10 days; because of clinical failure of a beta-lactam and confirmed resistant organisms, a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 500 mg OD or moxifloxacin 400 mg OD) is a guideline-endorsed alternative and is culture-concordant here. Source control is central to this refractory case: ENT performed endoscopically guided middle-meatal aspiration/drainage of the obstructed maxillary sinus, which both relieved the closed-space collection and yielded the culture that directed therapy. De-escalate to targeted oral therapy once susceptibilities returned. Reserve macrolides and TMP-SMX empirically given high pneumococcal resistance. Optimise glycaemic control. Escalate imaging/urgent ENT review if orbital or intracranial complications (periorbital swelling, diplopia, altered sensorium) develop.
contraindications: Avoid fluoroquinolones in pregnancy and use cautiously given tendon/QT/dysglycaemia risks, especially in a diabetic patient
Avoid amoxicillin monotherapy for treatment failure — inadequate against beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae
Avoid empiric macrolides/TMP-SMX for ABRS due to high pneumococcal resistance
Penicillin allergy would preclude amoxicillin-clavulanate — use doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone
edgeCases: Development of periorbital/orbital cellulitis, proptosis or ophthalmoplegia indicates orbital extension needing urgent contrast imaging and surgical drainage
In poorly controlled diabetes or immunosuppression, black eschar/necrotic turbinate or facial numbness should raise acute invasive fungal (mucormycosis) sinusitis — a surgical emergency
Frontal sinus involvement with forehead swelling (Pott's puffy tumour) or new neurological signs signals intracranial spread
expectedMaiK: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis is diagnosed clinically by symptoms >10 days or the double-sickening pattern with purulent discharge and facial pain; high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate is first-line, and treatment failure with confirmed beta-lactamase-producing/penicillin-non-susceptible organisms warrants escalation plus ENT sinus drainage for source control.
expectedNextQuestions: Any visual change, diplopia, periorbital swelling or altered behaviour to suggest orbital/intracranial complication?
Exactly which antibiotic, dose and duration was used first-line, and was there any partial response?
Recent antibiotic exposure, penicillin allergy status, and diabetes/glycaemic control?
Any dental pain or recent dental procedure suggesting an odontogenic source?
expectedInvestigations: Endoscopically guided middle-meatal/sinus aspirate for Gram stain, culture and susceptibilities

antibiotics: Levofloxacin 500 mg OD or moxifloxacin 400 mg OD (alternative for beta-lactam failure/allergy)

regressionAssertions: Engine should rank SINUSITIS as the top diagnosis given >10-day duration, double sickening, unilateral facial pain and purulent nasal discharge
Should not classify as simple viral URTI given bacterial ABRS criteria and antibiotic failure
Stewardship should recommend high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate first-line and flag amoxicillin monotherapy as inadequate for beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae
Should recommend ENT sinus aspiration/drainage (source control) for refractory disease and should not recommend empiric macrolide/TMP-SMX
Should prompt assessment for orbital/intracranial complications
